title: Introduction to Claude Code
summary: What Claude Code is, how the agentic loop works, its tools, the interfaces available, and how to make the most of the full ecosystem.

articles.title: Claude Code is a coding agent
articles.summary: It's not a chatbot. It's not autocomplete. It's an agent that makes decisions, takes actions, and verifies results.

blocks.content: Claude Code is a coding agent. It's not a chatbot you ask things of and copy the answer from. It's not line-by-line autocomplete. It's an agent that makes decisions, takes actions on your project, and verifies the results.

rows.value: Gives you answers. You copy, paste, adapt. Loses context. Doesn't know what files you have.
Autocompletes. Suggests the next line. Doesn't understand the project. Doesn't execute or verify.
Works with you. Reads your entire codebase. Edits multiple files. Executes and verifies.

articles.title: The agentic loop
articles.summary: How Claude Code processes each task: plans, uses real tools, evaluates the result, and repeats until done.

subsections.title: The five phases of the loop

blocks.content: Every task you give Claude Code goes through a cycle that repeats until completion. It's not a single response: it's a loop of action and evaluation.

items.title: Prompt
items.body: You describe the task. The more context and constraints you give, the better.

items.title: Plans
items.body: Claude decides the steps needed to complete the task.

items.title: Tool
items.body: Reads files, edits code, runs bash commands. Real actions, not simulations.

items.title: Evaluates
items.body: Analyzes the result of the action taken.

items.title: Done?
items.body: If not → repeats from Plans. If so → responds with the result.

blocks.content: Every iteration of the loop uses real tools: reads files, runs commands, edits code. It's not a simulation.

articles.title: The agent's tools
articles.summary: The internal tools Claude Code uses to interact with your project: read, edit, execute, search, and delegate.

items.title: Read
items.body: Reads files in your project. Can read the entire codebase to understand context.

items.title: Write / Edit
items.body: Creates or modifies files. Edit sends only the diff; Write rewrites the whole file.

items.title: Bash
items.body: Runs any terminal command: tests, builds, git, scripts, etc.

items.title: Glob / Grep
items.body: Searches for files by pattern and text within the project. Equivalent to find + grep.

items.title: Task
items.body: Delegates work to specialized subagents for parallel or complex tasks.

items.title: WebFetch
items.body: Fetches content from URLs. Useful for reading external documentation or APIs.

rows: Grep
Searches for a pattern within file contents (function names, error messages, imports)
When you know what text to search for but not which file it's in — finding every caller of a function
Glob
Finds files by path or name pattern (doesn't look at content)
When you know the shape of the filename — every `**/*.test.tsx`, every `config/*.yaml`
Read
Loads the full contents of a specific file
When you've already identified the exact file (via Grep or Glob) and need to see it whole to understand context
Edit
Modifies a specific section of a file, anchored on a unique piece of text
Surgical changes to existing files — safer than rewriting the whole file
Write
Creates a new file, or fully rewrites an existing one
New files, or when Edit fails because the anchor text isn't unique in the file
Bash
Runs shell commands: tests, builds, git, scripts
Any action that isn't directly reading/writing files — running the test suite, making a commit

blocks.content: Fallback pattern: if Edit fails because the text meant to anchor the change appears more than once in the file (non-unique match), the reliable alternative is Read to load the full file and Write to rewrite it with the change already applied — instead of insisting with increasingly long and fragile text anchors.

Typical exploration flow: start with Grep to find entry points (a function, an error, a keyword), use Read to follow imports and trace the flow from there, and only then decide what to modify. Reading the entire codebase file by file from the start wastes context on information irrelevant to the task.

articles.title: One agent, multiple interfaces
articles.summary: Claude Code is available in the terminal, VS Code/Cursor, web, and the desktop app. Each interface has its own advantages.

items.title: Terminal (CLI)
items.body: The full experience. All features. Ideal for power users.

items.title: VS Code / Cursor
items.body: Visual inline diffs. Checkpoints and rewind. The recommended option for the course.

items.title: Web (claude.ai/code)
items.body: No local install. For long-running tasks. From any device.

items.title: Desktop App
items.body: Parallel sessions. Visual diffs. Scheduled tasks (crons).

articles.title: What can you do with Claude Code?
articles.summary: A tour of the main capabilities: features, debugging, tests, refactoring, git, security, and automation.

items.title: Build complete features

items.title: Explore codebases
items.body: Understand projects you don't know: what each part does, how they connect.

items.title: Debug errors

items.title: Manage Git

articles.title: The ecosystem: more than a chat
articles.summary: Claude Code is a complete system: CLAUDE.md, MCP, Hooks, Subagents, Skills, and the Agent SDK all work together.

blocks.content: Claude Code isn't just a chat with a model. It's an ecosystem of components that combine to produce advanced behaviors and automation.

items.title: CLAUDE.md
items.body: Persistent project memory. Claude always reads it at the start of every session.

items.title: MCP
items.body: Model Context Protocol. Connection to external tools: databases, APIs, services.

items.title: Hooks
items.body: Event-based automation. Scripts that run before/after Claude's actions.

items.title: Subagents
items.body: Specialized AI teams. Claude can delegate tasks to parallel agents.

items.title: Skills
items.body: Reusable capabilities. Custom workflows invoked on demand.

items.title: Agent SDK
items.body: Programmatic use as a library. For integrating Claude Code into your own applications.

articles.title: What Claude Code is NOT
articles.summary: Setting the right expectations: Claude Code is a productivity multiplier, not a replacement for the developer or a magic fix.

rows.value: It doesn't make business decisions or understand the full context of your product.
It makes mistakes. Its proposals are a first draft you review.
"Just do it" without context produces generic results. Context and constraints are key.
Without permissions configured it can run destructive commands. Set up the sandbox.
Speeds up what you already know how to do. Amplifies your capabilities.

rows.key: A first draft that YOU review
rows.value: Always review the diff before accepting. Claude proposes, you decide.
Give it the project's CLAUDE.md, the exact error, the technical constraints.
Use settings.json, sandbox, and allow/deny rules to control what it can do.

blocks.content: The golden rule: Claude proposes, you decide. Always review the diff before accepting.

articles.title: Parallelizing Claude Code with worktrees
articles.summary: Run several Claude Code sessions at the same time without changes colliding, using git worktrees.

subsections.title: The problem: one session, one checkout

blocks.content: Two Claude Code sessions working on the same directory compete for the same files: if one is halfway through a feature and the other is fixing a bug, changes collide. A git worktree is a separate checkout (its own directory and its own branch) that shares the same repository's history — each session edits its own set of files, without conflict.

blocks.code:
claude --worktree feature-auth
# in another terminal, with a different name:
claude --worktree fix-bug-123

blocks.content: Each call creates the worktree under `.claude/worktrees/<name>/` on a new `worktree-<name>` branch, and starts the session there. When an unnamed session ends with no pending changes, Claude Code deletes the worktree on its own; if there's uncommitted work, it asks before deleting.

rows: The .git directory and its history
The working files (working tree)
Approved permissions ("don't ask again")
The active branch
Plugins installed at the project level
Untracked files (.env, etc. — unless in .worktreeinclude)

blocks.title: A new worktree is a clean checkout
blocks.content: It doesn't bring gitignored files like .env. For those files to automatically appear in every new worktree, declare a .worktreeinclude file at the project root, using .gitignore syntax.

The same mechanism applies to subagents: adding `isolation: worktree` to the frontmatter of a subagent defined in `.claude/agents/`, that subagent always runs in its own temporary worktree. Useful for agents that apply mechanical changes to many files (large refactors) in parallel with the main session, without risking the checkout the user is currently looking at.

blocks.title: Worktrees vs. subagents: they isolate different things
blocks.content: A worktree isolates files on disk. A subagent (see Subagents) isolates conversation context. They're complementary, not alternatives: you can have a subagent that also runs in its own worktree when its work involves editing files in parallel with the rest of the session.

`claude --worktree` handles creating and cleaning up the worktree, but not the final step: bringing the finished work on the `worktree-<name>` branch back into the main branch is still a normal git merge, done from the root checkout once the work in the worktree is committed.

# from the root checkout, with the worktree's work already committed
git merge worktree-feature-auth

If several parallel sessions touched related areas of the code, the merge can produce conflicts. Instead of resolving them by hand, you can ask Claude Code to resolve them — it has read access to both branches and can reason about which change from each side should be kept, instead of applying a mechanical resolution based only on the conflict markers.

This step lends itself to the same Custom commands pattern (see Rules) used for worktree creation: a `.claude/commands/merge-worktree.md` command parameterized with `$ARGUMENTS` can chain "check the worktree's latest commit → return to the root → merge the branch → resolve conflicts if any appear" into a single invocation, instead of repeating the sequence by hand every time a parallel session finishes.

articles.title: Effective debugging with Claude Code
articles.summary: The reproduce → diagnose → fix → verify pattern, and how to get Claude Code to follow it instead of proposing patches blindly.

blocks.content: A bug isn't solved by a plausible-sounding explanation or a reasonable-looking patch: it's solved when the failing behavior can be reproduced, and after applying the fix, it no longer occurs. Claude Code performs better at debugging when the session is structured as a closed loop, not a single question-and-answer.

items.title: Reproduce
items.body: Give Claude the exact command that triggers the error (not just the pasted message), so it can run it and see the full stack trace itself.

items.title: Diagnose
items.body: Let it explore the relevant code and propose a root cause before touching anything — asking for the diagnosis as a separate step prevents it from jumping straight to a superficial patch.

items.title: Fix
items.body: Apply the fix. If the bug is reproducible with a test, ask first for a failing test that captures the identified cause, and only then the fix that makes it pass — that way the bug can't reappear without a test catching it.

items.title: Verify
items.body: Run the original reproduction again (not just the test suite) to confirm the reported symptom actually disappeared.

blocks.title: Context that changes the diagnosis
blocks.content: Saying whether the error is intermittent or consistent completely changes which hypotheses are plausible — a race condition and a deterministic bug are investigated differently. That detail is rarely mentioned spontaneously and is always worth giving.

subsections.title: Automating parts of the loop with hooks

blocks.content: Asking Claude to "run the tests after every change" depends on it remembering to do so every turn. A PostToolUse hook that automatically runs the relevant test after each Edit makes that step deterministic — it doesn't matter whether Claude asks for it or not, the verification loop happens regardless. See the Hooks System for the full configuration.

subsections.title: Autonomous debugging: from interactive session to continuous monitoring

blocks.content: Everything above assumes an interactive session: a human brings the error. But the same reproduce → diagnose → fix → verify loop can run without anyone triggering it by hand, if Claude Code has access to where the error lives. By connecting an observability MCP server (for example, one that exposes CloudWatch, Sentry, or Datadog) as a tool, Claude can directly ask "what errors happened in the last 24 hours?", identify which ones deserve a fix, apply the correction with the same loop as always, and open a pull request — without the error ever being reported by a human first.

MCP isn't the only way to give it that access. The simpler variant, with no server in between, is having the CI job itself fetch the logs with the provider's CLI (`aws logs tail`, `gcloud logging read`, etc.) and pass them as text to a headless Claude Code invocation (see CI headless in Rules for the `-p` / `--output-format json` / `--max-turns` trio). A daily GitHub Actions cron following that pattern — checkout → install dependencies → fetch the last 24h of logs → ask Claude to analyze, deduplicate, and fix whatever it finds → open the PR — is quicker to set up than a dedicated MCP server when this workflow is the only consumer of those logs.

blocks.title: What to scope down so this cron doesn't become a problem
blocks.content: Read-only AWS permissions on CloudWatch, never write access to infrastructure. A cap on the number of errors processed per run so it doesn't exceed the context window. Deduplication before the logs reach Claude, so the same already-reported error doesn't get reopened every day. Repository write permissions scoped to opening the PR, not merging it. And running during off-peak hours if the log fetch competes for quota with real traffic.

rows: Routines
Cloud, managed by Anthropic
Runs even if your machine is off; can be triggered on a schedule or by GitHub/API events
Desktop App scheduled tasks
Your machine, via the desktop app
Needs direct access to local files, tools, or uncommitted changes
GitHub Actions
Your CI pipeline
Tasks tied to repo events (PR opened) or a cron that already lives alongside the rest of the CI config
/loop
The current CLI session
Fast polling while a session stays open; stops when a new conversation starts

blocks.title: The human doesn't disappear, they move to the PR gate
blocks.content: This pattern doesn't remove human review: it moves it from "before Claude investigates" to "before merging." Claude still proposes (the PR), a person still decides (the merge) — the project's golden rule (Claude proposes, you decide) doesn't change, only the point in the process where the human steps in changes.

articles.title: Structured workflows: Planning-First and Test-Driven
articles.summary: Two multi-step sequences that turn an ambiguous task into verifiable steps before any production code gets written: plan first without implementing, or define the tests first without implementing.

subsections.title: Why a single message isn't enough for complex tasks

blocks.content: Asking Claude Code to "implement feature X" in a single message works for small, well-scoped changes. For multi-file features, or for domains with non-obvious design decisions, that same message produces inconsistent results across attempts — not because Claude "didn't understand," but because the task admits more than one valid interpretation, and Claude picks one without the developer getting a chance to correct course before any code gets written. Two step sequences solve this in different ways: sign off on the plan before touching code, or sign off on the tests before touching code.

items.title: Feed context
items.body: Ask Claude to read the files relevant to the feature — examples of similar existing code, reusable helpers, the module that's about to be extended.

items.title: Plan without implementing
items.body: Describe what needs to be built but explicitly ask for no code yet, only the step-by-step plan. Turning on Plan Mode (see Plan Mode and headless CI) enforces this mechanically instead of relying on Claude respecting a prose instruction.

items.title: Implement
items.body: Once the plan is solid and has been reviewed, ask for the implementation. Claude already has the context and the planning done — the code comes out aligned with what was agreed on, not with the first possible reading of the original request.

blocks.content: The leverage point of this workflow is step 2: reviewing and correcting a plan is far cheaper than reviewing and correcting a full implementation that took the wrong approach.

items.title: Feed context
items.body: Same as Planning-First: share the relevant files so the proposed tests reflect the system's actual behavior, not a generic version of it.

items.title: Ask for test cases, no code yet
items.body: Ask Claude to think through test cases — including edge cases — before writing any implementation. This separates "what the solution must satisfy" from "how it gets built," and surfaces edge cases the developer hadn't anticipated.

items.title: Implement only the relevant tests
items.body: From the proposed list, pick the cases that actually apply to this feature — not everything Claude suggests is necessarily relevant — and ask for them to be implemented as tests that will fail (there's no code yet that passes them).

items.title: Implement code that passes the tests
items.body: Only at this step does Claude write the implementation, iterating until the selected tests pass. "Done" is defined upfront by the tests, not by a visual read of the code.

blocks.content: This workflow takes more upfront effort than asking for the feature directly, but the result is more robust because edge cases end up captured as verifiable tests before a single line of implementation exists to accidentally pass them.

rows.value: Structural changes: which files to touch, in what order, what could break

rows.key: What it forces a decision on upfront

rows.value: Plan Mode — blocks execution until the plan is approved
Business logic with precise rules and edge cases: calculations, validation, parsers

rows.key: What it forces a decision on upfront
rows.value: The expected behavior, case by case
The tests themselves — there's no way to call it "done" without them passing

blocks.content: They're not mutually exclusive: for a large feature with complex business logic, it's common to plan the overall structure first (Planning-First) and then apply Test-Driven within that structure for the module with the trickiest rules. The loop in Effective debugging with Claude Code uses a variant of this same principle — writing a failing test first for the identified root cause — but applied to existing bugs instead of new features.
